site.reason: Python reads whole lines; Java Scanner reads whitespace-separated tokens, and nextLine() after nextInt() returns the rest of the current line, often an empty string.

flags.reasoning: Python's input() reads a whole line, whereas Java's Scanner.nextInt() reads the next whitespace-delimited token. Because only one integer is read and no nextLine() follows nextInt(), there is no leftover-newline bug, and for valid single-integer inputs both programs behave the same.

site.reason: Python int() accepts any size; Java Integer.parseInt and Scanner.nextInt throw for values outside int range, so the translation must choose int, long or BigInteger.

flags.suggestion: Change line 8 to long n = input.nextLong(); (or use BigInteger with input.nextBigInteger() and BigInteger arithmetic if inputs beyond 64-bit signed range must be supported).

site.reason: Python % takes the divisor's sign (-7 % 2 is 1); Java % takes the dividend's (-7 % 2 is -1). Math.floorMod matches Python.

flags.assumption: Java uses Math.log(n) / Math.log(2) % 1 != 0 on line 10, assuming floating-point division of natural logs yields an exact integer for powers of 2 and that n >= 1; for n = 536870912 (2^29), Math.log(n) / Math.log(2) evaluates to 29.000000000000004, making % 1 != 0 true and causing an infinite loop instead of printing 1 as Python does.
flags.suggestion: Replace Math.log(n) / Math.log(2) % 1 != 0 on line 10 with (n & (n - 1)) != 0 (and throw an exception if n <= 0 to match Python's ValueError on non-positive inputs).
flags.reasoning: For n >= 1, the dividend is non-negative so the sign difference of % does not trigger, and for n <= 0 Python throws ValueError while Java produces -Infinity/NaN and loops infinitely. Even for valid positive powers of 2 such as n = 536870912 (2^29), Math.log(536870912) / Math.log(2) produces 29.000000000000004 in IEEE 754 double, so % 1 != 0 evaluates to true, n becomes 0, and subsequent iterations loop forever on NaN != 0.

site.reason: Python ints have unlimited precision; Java int and long arithmetic wraps silently on overflow (1000000 * 1000000 as an int is -727379968).

flags.reasoning: Because n is read as a 32-bit signed int on line 8 and line 12 is only reached when n >= 1 (in valid execution), the exponent is at most 30, and 2^30 = 1073741824 fits exactly in double and within 32-bit int without overflow.
